Deface

/dih-FAYS/ - rhymes with place · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Deface means to ruin or injure the appearance of something.

Election posters seldom survive a weekend downtown before somebody defaces them with devil horns and blacked-out teeth.

Worked Example

The foundry poured the mayor's statue in 1911, and for ninety years the only marks on it were rain streaks. Then came the decade of paint pens. The parks department now waxes the bronze twice a year, because ink lifts off wax but bites into raw metal, and every tag ground away takes a sliver of the sculptor's chisel work with it.

Deface is the exact word for what the taggers do, because it means to ruin or injure the appearance of something — the statue still stands, still holds its shape; what suffers is its face, the surface the city actually sees. Destroying it would take it away entirely; defacing it leaves the thing whole and makes you wince at it.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

disfigure: Disfigure is the deeper injury — a face or form marred for good, so the shape itself reads differently ever after. Deface can be one ugly mark on a surface; the thing underneath is still whole and still itself.

mar: Mar is the general spoiler: it can spoil an event, a mood, a finish — almost anything, and sometimes only slightly. Deface is stricter: it needs a physical surface you can see, and it injures the way that surface looks.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

beautify: dress a surface up

repair: put the damage right

Where it sits · how much harm the object suffers — smudge → deface → destroy

smudge vs. deface: A smudge is far milder than defacement — the smallest insult a surface can take, gone with one wipe; to deface something leaves a mark that will not wipe away.

destroy vs. deface: Destroy goes further than deface — a defaced mural still hangs there, hurt but present; a destroyed one is simply gone.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — de-

Prefix — de-: off, away

Root — face

Root — face: the front a thing shows

Put it together

Put it together: De- (off) + face = to take the face off. Old French desfacier built it exactly that way, and English kept the logic: what a defacer attacks is not the thing but its face — the surface it presents to the world.

Use the root in a new word: surface

Use the root in a new word: surface: A surface is literally the "upper face" — sur- (above) + face — the face a thing turns toward you.

Root Check

Word Choice

neutral / civic

Deface is the word on park signs and museum placards, and it is strict about its object: surfaces and appearances. To spoil an occasion or a mood, reach for mar; to lower a thing's worth, this unit's debase; and when the injured surface is sacred — an altar, a gravestone — the graver word is desecrate.
